parts.note: French eighteen, given a few more years, will become French twenty-one, which also names a card game

explanation.surface: A French number looks ahead to what it will become.
explanation.walkthrough: Dix-huit is French for eighteen; three years on, an eighteen-year-old is twenty-one, and the French for that is also the name of the card game better known as pontoon or blackjack.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for twenty-one names the card game played to reach that total, and eighteen grows into twenty-one.

explanation.surface: A sad spot to say farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase 'vale of tears' names a sorrowful earthly valley, and the Latin farewell word means goodbye.

parts.note: both the composer and the painter produced works called nocturnes, evoking night

explanation.surface: A question about the impression a composer and a painter make.
explanation.walkthrough: Chopin wrote piano nocturnes and James Whistler painted views of the Thames at night called nocturnes.
explanation.definitionFit: Their nocturnes create a night-time mood, an effect of darkness and evening.

clue.text: Hardly the wink to tip the man with the breathalyser!

definitions.text: Hardly the wink to tip the man with the breathalyser!

parts.words: Hardly the wink to tip the man with the breathalyser!
parts.note: a word that comes before winks in the name of a game also means slightly drunk, not what a driver wants a policeman to see

explanation.surface: A motorist shouldn't signal to the traffic policeman testing breath.
explanation.walkthrough: Add 'winks' and you have the counter game; on its own it is British slang for slightly drunk, which a breath test would reveal.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a little tipsy, which is just what a breath-testing policeman checks for.

clue.text: Keepsake is all right in X's keeping

indicators.note: the numeral holds the other piece in its keeping, so it goes round it

parts.note: X is the Roman numeral ten
all right is OK

explanation.surface: A memento is fine while held by someone called X.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' puts OK inside TEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake is a memento or small symbolic gift.

clue.text: "'Tis Apollo comes leading His choir, the ——" (Arnold)

definitions.text: "'Tis Apollo comes leading His choir, the ——" (Arnold)

parts.words: "'Tis Apollo comes leading His choir, the ——" (Arnold)
parts.note: a line from Matthew Arnold with the closing word missing; the solver supplies the number of the Muses

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse about Apollo with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: From Arnold's Empedocles on Etna: Apollo leads the Muses, who are nine in number.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muses who sing with Apollo number nine in Greek myth.

explanation.surface: Someone confessed to having the goods on them.
explanation.definitionFit: To own up is to confess, so admitted; and something possessed is held by its proprietor.

parts.note: costs covering a whole business, like an umbrella held above the head

explanation.surface: Asking what fees for an umbrella are like.
explanation.walkthrough: Umbrella charges are the general running costs of a business; an umbrella also sits above you.
explanation.definitionFit: General running costs are called by this term, and an umbrella is held above the head.

parts.note: what people are called is the usual way they are told apart

explanation.surface: Ways of proving who you are.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of 'Means' rearrange to the answer, though no word signals an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: What a person or thing is called identifies them.

clue.text: " The tocsin of the soul " to Byron

definitions.text: " The tocsin of the soul " to Byron

parts.words: " The tocsin of the soul " to Byron
parts.note: Byron's phrase in Don Juan for the bell summoning people to the evening meal

explanation.surface: Byron's poetic name for an alarm bell of the spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: A tocsin is an alarm bell; Byron in Don Juan called the call to dinner 'the tocsin of the soul'.
explanation.definitionFit: Byron gave this bell, rung to summon a household to its meal, a grand alarm-call title.

clue.text: " His silver skin-- -with his golden blood " (Macbeth)

definitions.text: " His silver skin-- -with his golden blood " (Macbeth)

parts.words: " His silver skin-- -with his golden blood " (Macbeth)
parts.note: a line from Macbeth with a word missing; the solver supplies the word Shakespeare wrote

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Macbeth describes the murdered Duncan: 'His silver skin laced with his golden blood', streaked or threaded with it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's verb means streaked or threaded through, the blood marking the skin like lacing.

parts.note: the idiom for a miserable existence is read literally: a man who walks dogs on a lead and runs their lives

explanation.surface: Sympathy for some poor wretch having a miserable time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leads a dog's life' usually means suffers; here he literally leads dogs, as the keeper of a kennels does.
explanation.definitionFit: A man employed at kennels looks after and walks the dogs, so he leads them through life.

parts.note: the verb that means pondering something over carefully is also the verb for heating wine with spices

explanation.surface: Someone heats wine with great care and attention.
explanation.walkthrough: One verb does both jobs: thinking something over at length, and heating wine with sugar and spice.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both pondering at length and spicing and heating wine, so studious thought and warm wine meet in one word.

clue.text: Step taken when pursued by a Frenchman ?

explanation.surface: A dancer takes a step while a Frenchman follows close behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A gliding dance step bears this name, and in French the same word is the past participle meaning hunted or chased.

parts.note: a marriage certificate seems to show correct bonds

explanation.surface: Wedding papers point to shared belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as 'proper ties', the lawful bonds of a marriage certificate; whole, it means things owned.
explanation.definitionFit: Things owned, such as land and houses, are possessions.

clue.text: The bird took a header, American fashion

explanation.surface: A bird plunged head first like an American.
explanation.definitionFit: The pigeon-like bird of peace, and in American usage the past tense of dive, meaning plunged head first.

explanation.surface: A short report of noise everywhere.
explanation.definitionFit: A bell's peal is a sound, and a circle or hoop runs all round.

clue.text: Dangerously situated — up a gumtree no doubt

parts.note: someone up a tree is literally sitting on a branch, which is the source of the idiom for being exposed

explanation.surface: Someone stuck up a tree is in a precarious spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up a gum tree' is itself slang for being in trouble, and anyone up a tree is sitting on a branch.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes being exposed in a risky position, like someone stranded on a branch.

clue.text: You'll find the island in situ!

indicators.note: you must find the island by working over the letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Encouragement that the place is just where it should be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'find' rearranges SITU; Uist is a pair of islands in the Outer Hebrides of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: North and South Uist are islands in Scotland's Outer Hebrides.

clue.text: " Broad-based upon her people's will, And compassed by the —— sea" (Tennyson)

definitions.text: " Broad-based upon her people's will, And compassed by the —— sea" (Tennyson)

parts.words: " Broad-based upon her people's will, And compassed by the —— sea" (Tennyson)
parts.note: lines from Tennyson's dedication to Queen Victoria with the adjective for the sea missing

explanation.surface: Tennyson praises Britain, founded on popular will and ringed by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: From Tennyson's 'To the Queen': the realm is 'compassed by the inviolate sea', the sea that keeps it unbreached.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's adjective means unbreached and secure, the sea protecting Britain from invasion.

parts.note: writers deep in thought suck the tips of their pens, so they lick nibs

explanation.surface: Societies for writers who think hard.
explanation.walkthrough: A niblick is an old golf club, roughly a nine iron; split it as 'nib licks', what a pensive writer does.
explanation.definitionFit: An old-fashioned golf club for lofted shots, roughly the modern nine iron.

parts.note: matey is pally and the foolish are asses, so the two run together as one sound for straw mattresses

explanation.surface: A friendly but silly couple share a bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'pally asses' quickly and you get the plural of a straw mattress, the bedfellow that lies under you.
explanation.definitionFit: Straw mattresses are what a sleeper lies with in bed, so they are bedfellows of a kind.

clue.text: "All constraint, Except what wisdom lays on —— men, Is ——" (Cowper)

definitions.text: "All constraint, Except what wisdom lays on —— men, Is ——" (Cowper)

parts.words: "All constraint, Except what wisdom lays on —— men, Is ——" (Cowper)
parts.note: a quotation from William Cowper with the same word missing twice; the solver supplies it

explanation.surface: Cowper says that all restraint not imposed by wisdom on wicked people is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Cowper's line reads 'All constraint, except what wisdom lays on evil men, is evil' from The Task.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet uses the word both as an adjective for wicked men and as a noun for wrongdoing.

parts.note: small fish used as bait, as in the proverb about throwing one to catch a mackerel

explanation.surface: Attractive small swimmers.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a sprat to catch a mackerel' means a small outlay to win a big prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Small fish of the herring family serve as bait in the proverb, so they entice.

clue.text: Wife with a frisky lad is apt to be coarse!

parts.note: Eve was made from Adam's rib, so a wife is jokingly called a rib

indicators.note: a frisky creature jumps about, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A married woman who goes off with a playful young man risks vulgar gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'frisky' rearranges LAD as ALD, placed after RIB, the old name for a wife.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude, vulgar humour is described as coarse.

clue.text: What one copper in bed did with his time !

indicators.note: one and a copper go inside the bed

parts.note: taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I
D, from the Latin denarius, was the old British penny, a copper coin

explanation.surface: A policeman lying in bed waits for his shift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ID inside BED; 'copper' looks like a policeman but is a penny. To bide one's time is to wait patiently.
explanation.definitionFit: Waiting patiently for the right moment is biding one's time.

explanation.surface: A bloom that a poet loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Campion was an Elizabethan poet and songwriter, and the pink or white wildflower of hedgerows shares his surname.

clue.text: Its day, one of uncertain glory.

definitions.text: Its day, one of uncertain glory.

parts.words: Its day, one of uncertain glory.
parts.note: Shakespeare's Two Gentlemen of Verona speaks of the uncertain glory of a day in a changeable spring month

explanation.surface: A day whose splendour may not last.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is 'the uncertain glory of an April day', spring weather turning from sun to showers.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare names this showery spring month as the one whose days shine uncertainly.

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work

explanation.surface: Someone is busy on the mountain top.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitting on top of something is being at its peak.

clue.text: They provide refreshment in two directions

parts.note: north and south are two compass points

explanation.surface: Places offering drinks to travellers going either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Taverns and hostelries serve food and drink to travellers.

parts.note: a hand pointing the way is one kind of sign showing where to look

explanation.surface: A hand points the way.
explanation.definitionFit: A pointer, dial needle or signpost hand shows a direction or reading, like a finger aimed at something.

parts.note: one is the article a
a win counts as a gain

explanation.surface: Win another victory.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something once more is repeating it.

parts.note: players chosen for a match form the opposing teams

explanation.surface: A group of selected men.
explanation.definitionFit: Teams of players picked to face each other are the two teams of a game.

clue.text: O, her slip's showing, say the shoeshine boys

indicators.note: the letters show themselves in a new arrangement, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the letter O, her, and slip's read as slip is, giving slips

explanation.surface: Boys shining shoes call out that a woman's petticoat is visible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing' rearranges O, HER and SLIPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoeshine boys make shoes shine by buffing them.
